zh: 映射值都在 1..9，所以子串的平均值也在 1..9；和能被长度整除，等价于平均值恰好是某个整数 k∈{1..9}。
固定 k，把每个映射值减去 k，问题变成统计和为 0 的子串，也就是统计相等的前缀和对数；九个 k 分别统计后相加，同一子串只会在它的平均值那一轮被计入。
按表把字母映射为数字（ab→1，cde→2，…，xyz→9，注意第一组只有两个字母）；对每个 k 用频次数组记前缀和（偏移 8n 避免负下标），先登记空前缀，每到一个新前缀先累加相同前缀的次数再登记；九轮结果相加输出。
en: Mapped values lie in 1..9, so a substring's average also lies in 1..9; the sum is divisible by the length exactly when the average is some integer k in {1..9}.

Fix k and subtract k from every mapped value; the task becomes counting zero-sum substrings, i.e. pairs of equal prefix sums. Count for each of the nine values of k and add them; a substring is counted only in the round of its own average.

Map letters with the table (ab→1, cde→2, ..., xyz→9; note the first group has only two letters); for each k keep a frequency array of prefix sums (offset by 8n to avoid negative indices), register the empty prefix first, and at each new prefix add the count of equal earlier prefixes before registering it; print the total of the nine rounds.

explanationEn:
## Fixed original text and the basis for recovering the missing mapping

The fixed upstream file fastprep/Wayfair/wayfair-number-of-divisible-substrings.md already defines the problem in full: map letters to digits and count the contiguous non-empty substrings whose sum of mapped values is divisible by the length. The length is 1..2000 with only lowercase English letters, and the three original examples asdf→6, bdh→4, abcd→6 are complete. The original mapping image points to a path on the author's own machine and cannot be read from there; the starter explicitly references LC2950.

The site recovered the full mapping from the Problem Source image published on that FastPrep original problem page, actually inspecting the nine-cell table, the examples and the constraints item by item, without guessing the table from the title or reverse-engineering it from curated code. Source image URL: https://storage.googleapis.com/fastprepoa.appspot.com/problem_source_images/wayfair-number-of-divisible-substrings.jpg . The saved copy is content/oa-judge/source-images/wayfair-2-original.jpg, with SHA256 63d7c5e6186ab7fd56f35a9c80eda7744b7bb327bf68aa2758c43528439090c8. This image is public source material obtained separately and does not pose as the image in the fixed Git snapshot.

The full table is: 1→ab; 2→cde; 3→fgh; 4→ijk; 5→lmn; 6→opq; 7→rst; 8→uvw; 9→xyz. Note that the first group has only two letters, not three per group, and it is not a phone keypad. Count by position: repeated content at different positions is counted separately; substrings are contiguous and non-empty, not subsequences or de-duplicated distinct strings.

The site's input is one lowercase string without quotes, of length 1..2000; the output is the number of qualifying substrings. The full original range is kept, empty strings are not allowed, and the three original examples are unchanged. The valid substrings of asdf are a, s, d, f, as, sdf; for bdh they are b, d, h, bdh; for abcd they are a, b, c, d, ab, cd.

## Approach

Each mapped value is in 1..9, so the average of a non-empty substring is also in 1..9. The sum is divisible by the length if and only if the average is an integer k∈{1,...,9}. After fixing k, subtract k from every value, and the problem becomes counting substrings with sum 0.

Scan this transformed array while maintaining prefix sums. A substring [l,r) has sum 0 if and only if the prefix sums satisfy P[l]=P[r]. The frequency array first registers the empty prefix 0 once; for each new prefix, first add the number of earlier equal prefixes to the answer, then register the current prefix. Scan once for each of the nine values of k and accumulate the answer. Each step changes the prefix by at most 8 in absolute value, so prefix sums lie in [−8n,8n]; access the array with an offset of 8n, no hashing needed.

## Proof of correctness

For any non-empty substring, let S be its original mapped sum and L>0 its length. If S is divisible by L, the integer k=S/L must be in 1..9, and in that round the transformed sum is S−kL=0. If some round's transformed sum is 0, then S=kL, so the substring qualifies. The average is unique, so a valid substring appears in exactly one round and is never counted across rounds twice.

For fixed k, when the scan reaches right end r, the frequency array holds only prefixes strictly before r. Each left end l whose prefix equals the current one corresponds to exactly one non-empty zero-sum substring; querying before registering excludes the empty substring with l=r. Every substring has a unique right end, so this round counts exactly the substrings with average k. Combining the nine rounds gives all valid substrings and only them, counted separately by position.

## Complexity and integers

The nine scans and clearing the frequency array are O(9n), so total time is O(n) and space O(n). The largest answer is n(n+1)/2, which is 2001000 at n=2000, reached when all mapped values are equal; the original int return type suffices. The reference accumulates in 64 bits and uses int for frequencies and prefix indices.

## Independent verification

An independent oracle uses a double loop over start and end, adding mapped values character by character and checking sum%length==0 directly, without average enumeration or prefix frequencies. The three original examples, 163 unique oracles, all 26 letters and the boundaries between adjacent groups are covered. In addition, all 1092 strings of length 1..6 over the letters acx were enumerated and the native reference was actually run on them. Full-length official cases cover all nine equal-value groups, a period of the whole alphabet, a reversed alphabet period, alternating lowest/highest values, adjacent mapping groups, random full alphabets and two extreme halves; the equal-value groups are independently rechecked with the closed form 2001000. The three negative controls respectively mis-assign the letter mapping, miss averages, and wrongly include the empty substring; each counts as killed only if it exits normally on all official cases.
